CONGREGATIONALISM AT WARRINGTON. The public recognition of the Rev. John Yonge, the successor to the Rev. G. S. Ramey, to the pastorate of Wycliffe, toe& place in that Church, on Thursday night, under the presidency of Rev. T. Willis, of Manchester. There was a large attendance of members of the church and the general public. Amongst those present were the Rev. G. S. Reaney, of Reading, the late pastor; Rev. B. Yates, of Rune= ; Rev. J. Hill, of St. Helens ; Rev. 'l'. W. Finn, of Lymm ; Rev. James Allatt. of Newton , Rev. G. Williams, of Rochdale; Rev. Lloyd Jones (Wesleyan), Rev. J. Wilkinson ,Itaptist, of Latchford), Bev. A. Harrison (Baptist), Rev. It. W. Thompson, Liverpool ; Rev. A. Kenworthy (Baptist), Mr. B. Eigby, J.P., Mr. R. W. Murray, Mr. Councillor Guest. Mr. Councillor Armitege, &c., and a large number of members of other Uhl istian churches in the town. After devotional exercises, The Rev. Teroeug Wrure said that occasion was a most important era in the history of that church, and he hoped io years to cerne it would be increwingly and Won e clearly shown, that the union whieh was that night celebrated between Mr. Yonge and his people, had been brought about by the great master and head of the church. (Hear, bear.) On occasions of that Sort ther. was considerable enthuei-sm displayed, and an inexperienced mind might infer things which were never realised, and though a more manifest feeling between themselves and their pastor might somewhat srubidde and be not so manifest and evidenced, yet in years and days to come it might be found that that feeling was quite as true if not truer and deeper than they had ever contemplated. (Hear, hear.) It was their duty to remember that in entering into that union not only had Mr. Yonge taken upon himself certain responsibilities and duties, but the members of the church and congregation had also undertaken duties and reap neibilinee, and it was just as the church recognised their own share of the responsibility, that they would find their relationship ' with their new pastor attenoed with the most gratifying results. (Hear, hear.) Tney Lad asked Mr. Yonge to become their pastor, and 10 such he would feel it his duty to preach the gospel to them. They must never forget that. He fit quite sure Mr. Yonge would be a pastor, and attend to pastm al duty, yet still his great duty would be to make known the unseerchable riches of Christ. If they did not see him as often as they liked yet if he broke the word of life to them successfully they must not complain. In fact his own experience was this—that people would dispense now and then with pastoral visitation, if only the pulpit was efficiently maintained. (Hear, hear.) They must always bear in mind that the minieter was net eirgaged to preach just as his congre- gation wanted him—he had to deliver what appeared to him to be God's message. On the other hand it was their duty to be thei 8 im ruing and evening to listen. (Hear.) What was wanted in all their congregations was a more re,..ular attendance at the means of Grace. They mnstnot be listless in their pews simply b3csuse the preacher was not pleasing them, for he was under no obligation to preach that which wool,' just please this person or the other. (Hear, hear.) If he were a faithful minister and servant of God, he would preach the message God had given him wuether men heard or not. (Heni' hear.) He trusted both minister and people would maintain each other's reputation, that the union celebrated that evening would be a source of joy to them all, and that out of it would spring mighty blessings upon themselves and on this town at large. (Cheers.) Mr. S. RIGBY, at the request a the Chairman, came forward and explained the circumstances which had led to Mr. Yonge'e appointment as pastor of that place. He said it would be known to many of them that in consequence of the ill-health of Mr. iteaney, their late pastor, he was compelled to remove from Warrington, and for a short time before his removal, nothing was anther from their thoughts than that any other Minister should be their pastor, so long as Mr. Reaney lived. (Hear, bear.) However, circumstances over which they had no control, led to the necessity of his removal, consequently, alter the pulpit was vacant, the Members of the Church assembled together and asked God's direction in seeking for another pastor. He be- lieved they prayed, and prayed earnestly that they might be so guided, and after due and proper notice had been given to the parties interested, the members of the Church met, and determined unanimously only to present one person they deemed eligible at one time, and whatever the opinion of the church might be, it ohould be so expressed so as to make no invidious die- Unction. There had been great unity of purpose be- tween the officers of the church and its members, as to the proposal to invite Mr. Yonge to preach in that Church, and the deacons after waiting for some indica- tion from the members as to their wishes in the matter, received an expression of, opinion most favourable to that gentleman's invitation. Subsequently after the various forms had been complied with, Mr. Yonge was Invited by the unanimous voice of the church to under- 4PaifiAladettaDeVlet.e' ' Igy.ll tit ire _ _aarlisUhr ies'ilh h' s -ac ' time of very great anxiety for the church, and he could not avoid expressing his gratitude on behalf of his fellow officers to all the members of the Church for the extremely great forbearance they had exercised towards their officers, and for the unanimity with which they had carried out the desires , of the Church, and for their patient waiting. (Hear, bear.) lhey might easily conceive their anxiety, ' when week after week the Church was still without a I pastor, but they waited patiently until the proper time came. It he had had any experience in churches and their government, he must say that Wycliffe presented an exarsple to all other churches; and while they bad exercised no undue haste, they had been exceed- ingly anxious and desirous to be settled as soon as pos- sible. (blear,lear.) They knew the necessity there was for this, owing to the energetic manner in which the services of the sanctuary had been conducted by their late minister, and LIS assiduous labeur generally. However, they were now about to reap the reward of their patience. He believed they had been wisely directed, and he was stating the unanimous opinion of the (facers and Church members when he said that they looked forward to great results; and they trusted that the labours which had been commenced in that place and continued for a long time with so much sue- cess, would go on and re..ouud to the honour and glory of the great Head of the Church. (Applause.) They expected great things. It was natural and right that they should. If they expected nothing, then they would get all they expecteu and no wore. (Laugh- ter.) He was one who he:d that view, and he was certainly very expectant. (Hear' hear.) With a population of 40,000. they ought to have large congre- gations. Their former mioister laboured hard not only to gain a large congregation but a steady con- gregation. He looked out tor the young, and had had striven to assemble them round him, to teach them, and to show them that the ways of religion were ways of pleasantness' and. her paths were paths of peace. (Hear, hear.) What they humbly prayed and hoped for was that their present minister should follow in Mr. Heaney's footsteps, and that he would not only Bee as the result of Lb preaching a large congregation, , but that it would not be the only congregation in the town gathered together under the denomination of Congregationalism, but that there should be other congregations, not merely of themselves, but of other religions denominations. (Hear, hear.) They were not aelfish ; what they wanted was that Satan should be rohbed of his disciples and that those who wor- shipped him now should ultimately be led to worship a loving and merciful God. (Loud cheers.) Ihe CHAIRMAN said they had heard with pleasure ' the statement from Mr. Rigby, and they would now listen to what Mr. Yonge had to say respecting his ac- ceptance of the pastorate. The Rev. J. YONGE, on rising to address the meet- ing, was most cordially received. His address, which was frequently applauded throughout, was as follows; The feelings with s.hich I dud myself in this position to-night are of a very mingled character; and I am lieneible of considerable difficulty in fulfilling my part Of the programme of this meeting. I can do no other than cast myself upon your forbearance and sympathy while I try briefly to state how it is that I find myself here, and what, now lam here, I desire to endeavour to do. Concerning the story of my coming to this church as its pastor, that part relating to the action of the Church itself has been already detailed. My part in the matter, were I nainutely to describe it, would Pro- bably appear to many somewhat strange and per. plexieg. I may say, however, that with considerable stubborness I resisted repeated invitations to pay a I visit to this place. I knew, of course, that it was '1 what is known amongst Us as "a vacant church." That phrase does not mean an empty building—not an empty pulpit. And consequently I knew that, how- ever ranch I might mean otherwise, certain individuals would,be sure to suppose from the fact of my occu- pying the pulpit, if only for a day, that I was not in- disposed to occupy it altogether. .I can most honestly affirm that I had no such desire. I did not regard myself as a "moveable" individual. Although I never Intended, as the phreae is, to live and die in Hey- wood, still nothing was farther from my desire or in- tention than to remove just now. Therefore I resisted with much obstinacy the invitation to preach here. I refused twice, but on the seconct occasion I felt that I had no right to be rude to gentlecueu who pre s ,ed for my Services; and furtuer, that in ruy obstinate ref Da l I might possibly be resisting a higher woe than either to,tai Or Lily own. And, in declining the secgornecl:: citation, was a day I could place at their disposal, it aea to themselves. This was in June last. I received a prompt reply from the secretary of the church, thank. ing me fur my offer, but stating that the deacons were not then wiscung to fix any arrangements for the month of August. I congratulated myself upon re- ceiving that letter, in that I had both shown myself disposed to be courteous and escaped an engagement which Iliad not the slightest wish to undertake. Only a short time passed, however, before a renewed appli- cation was received by rise, in which I was asked to Visit Wycliffe the first Sunday in August, the day I jrad previously named. I could not escape. I Mould If I had been able, But escape being impossible, I had $O OEM 01:aei aD4 PrlAChetif With PO Prigual

dissatisfaction; and my feeling, as I retired from this pulpit to the vestry at the close of the evening ser- vice, was that Wycliffe people would never wish to see or hear me again. To my surprise, however, I was asked that night by Mr. Rigby whether, if an invita- tion were forthcoming, I would come and be the pastor of this church. The quest on raised all the opposi- tion of my nature. It seemed to me a question so premature, so rash almost, that I could not deal with it- and without treating it at all kindly, I went to my room for the night. I did not rest, but passed the first of many sleepless nights which this Wycliffe Church haa already occasioned.me. The question was renewed in the morning, and as Mr. Rigby could. tell you, was rebutted by me as vigorously as I knew how. I distinctly told him both then verbally, and afterwards in writing that I would not say one word which wood ' warrant the church in taking any action with regard to me. And I thought, once more, and hoped I had done with Wycliffe. 'Three weeks passed away. I was rusticating in a little out of the way place some miles from Lancaster, where neither post office nor tele- graph station existed, and where I tried to forget the world and the church also. One noon' the 28th August, came a communication with the Warrington post mark, which made me fear the worst. And sure enough "the worst," as I then felt it, had come. I was invited, unanimously, to the pastorate of this church. My holiday, which had had a shadow of misgiving about it all along, was then utterly spoiled, and! found my- self face to face with 'one of the gravest anxieties I have ever encountered. lam aware that good. people, and even, shall I say, ministerial brethren, do exist who can hardly understand how I should feel any difficulty in deciding. I was told by some that if they hau been in my case they should not have had two thoughts on the subject. Such an offer, coming from such a church, in such a town as Warrington, in their opinion, only one decision was possible. "Of course," they said, "you will accept the call." Looking at the thing, as I did, from a standpeint very different from theirs, my feeling was for long nearly this "Of course, I shall do no such thing." The members of this con- gregation already are acquainted with the difficulty and hesitation I felt concerning this invitation. There are brethren in the ministry here to-night with whom I conferred on the matter, stating to them as impar- tially as I knew how, the cleims of my people at Hey- wood, and those of the church in this place. And they could tell you how doubtful they felt as to what my duty was. I was aware that in many respects both the town of Heywood, and the Independent Church there were not so important as the tows of Warring- ton and this Wycliffe Church. And I knew also that a minister's position here would, at least in a wordly sense, be what is called very comfortable. But, life for ten years in the midst of a united people, of a church that has grown and extended, and developed under his own hand, this makes a minister hesitate very ranch indeed before he severs thellbnnection. And it it be of the same disposition as myself, one" not given to change." one who can only work well where he fetli thoroughly at home, one who largely depends for his power upon the sympathy and affection of those among whom he labours, then a minister wiil think not twice but twenty times before he dissolves the rOlationship. It is with feelings of great thankful- ness that I can freely declare to-night that there was no reason whatever in my relationship with the church at Heywood which suggested a need for my leaving it; and there are those present from Heywood in this meeting who could confirm what now I Say. We had worked for nearly ten years harmoniously and prosperously together, and might, but for this church's action, have been so working to-day. It will, I think, be seen therefore that the call from this church put me in real difficulty. The call reached me on the 28th August, I accepted it on the 16th September. The interval was a time such as 1 never wish to know again. I was beset and torn with tempests on both sides. 'Strong, earnest, enthusiastic appeals from my oil friends. Constant, urgent, pertinacious application.from the people here. Those I applied to for advice were almost equally divided. My ultimate decision was the result of a combination of circumstances, such as I need not thus publicly explain, but which, on the whole, cast the balance in favour of my coining here. Now lam here I desire frankly to affirm, and! ani glad indeed that I am able to do it, that I believe I have made the right decision, but I wish to say also, that however reluc- tant I was to come, I desire to throw all my energies without reserve, without qualification, into the great nnd important -work that is laid upon me. For ten yeap.past I have lived for the Church at Heywood. I. gave it my love, my streneth, my time. I did my best for it. I am prepared now to do my beat for Wycliffe, and shall in time, I doubt not, be able to render it my hearty and devoted love. I have met already with such a general and generous kindness, that I feel persuaded that the time cannot be far dis- tant when my heart will find its home in this place. The work of the Pastor of this Church may well make the man tremble who takes it up. I confess I feel nervous on account of my predecessor. To have him present here this evening affords me a very true satis- faction, and I wish thus publicly to thank him for coming, especially as I can estimate that his visit will be at the cost of some personal feeling. I hope he will ever feel that a visit from ;tains to his old friends will be to me a source of very real pleasure, and that whenever he is disposed to look in upon his old home and associations, no one will more sincerely weloame him than myself. And yet, he is a man who, in some respects, fills me with a kind of tremor. During his ministry here, he showed himself a man of such mani- fold, and inventive, end unwearied activity, that! fear the comparison,or rather the contrast that may now pre ffilVitt4llA s 1 yu ilikelite"ann 'Klee Peaulr, ITU fccr -an v-e-ry' ordinary individual to occupy his place seems bath balct and dangerous. Still, i am not without hope, that even notwithstanding all this, I may be of use in this place. It will probably be seen that I have my own ideas and ways, even as Mr. Raattey had. To follow all his lines would for me be impossible. Therefore, I propose to make my own lines, and to work according to my own abilities, Such, indeed, is the Master's thought about us; if each works accord- ihg to his individual ability, then each works accept- ably and well. What knowledge I could gather of Wycliffe before! came, and that which! have gathered since, assures me, that there is great room for work. Numerous as is the congregation, and the school; though the workers be many and able; though the or- ganisations are very orderly and very successful, still it does appear to me that better days still may come to us—days of larger numbers, of increased workers, of wider usefulness and success. And what talent and power I may have shall be directed to the attainment of this end. First and foremost, ever and always, with me will stand this pulpit. My greatest Effart will be to make it useful ; as useful in its spiritual influ- ence as it is chaste and beautiful in its material ap- pearance. I hold firmly that a minister's first and , greatest work is his preaching. Some people say other- ! wise. They say, let the minister visit ; let him be active in the school, and the preaching will not matter much. People talk sometimes without properly un- derstanding what they talk about; and lam afraid that the ideas just alluded to may not unfairly be so regarded. There is a time for visiting the people; but it is not when the minister should be in his study. There is a time for activity in the Sunday school ; but work in the school must not trench on work for the pulpit. Christ commands the minister to preach. He nas never, so far as I know, commanded him to visit- nor has He commanded him to superintend the super- intendent or the Sunday school, or to take the leading part in teaching there. There is a great danger of ex- pecting the minister to do too much. The late Mr. Parkinson. of Itochcle le, used to say that, according to Paul, Christ gave some apostles, and some prophets. and some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers: tiat now, said he, members of tho churches require one man to do the work of all the five. Rather an im- possible requisition. There are machines that can do the work of fifty men, or fifty horses, or five hundred. But then they are made of iron Sr steel, and are im- pelled by steam. One man can only do one man's work ; if he does that well, then he fulfils all that can be required of him, I do not mean, however, to imply that I shall do nothing but preach. I think you will already have heard differently. I will visit as much as I can, sick cases, or cases of sorrow, as promptly as possible. But my growing conviction is that visitation is mainly the people's work. They should visit each other, and when special need is dis- covered for a pastoral visit, let their pastor be made acquainted with it. Further: I will yield a hearty sympathy to the Sunday School. I hope few Sundays will pass without my presence there. The success of the pulpit will be largely aided and accelerated by cordial and intimate relations between the Preacher and the Sunday School. I hope to succeed in making the scholars, young and old feel that they have an interest in the Preacher and the pulpit. For some years past services for young people have been a leading feature in my ministry, and experience en- courages me to continue my efforts in this direction. It is by such means that our children may be taught to love the sanctuary, and to feel that it is a place for them, as well ae for other people. Putting then the Pulpit and Preaching first my aim will he to cultivate personal sympathy between myself and the people; to care very specially for the young, to conciliate the Church, and to secure its becoming a pre-eminently working Church. One great token of the success of the Pulpit will appear in the industry of the pew. Christ's call is a call to service, as well as salvation. I hope, also, to hold myself, and to encourage on the part of this Church, the friendliest relationships tower(' s all other societies of believers in the Lord Christ Jesus. The fact that lam Indepen- dent, and that this Church is such, need be no barrier to hearty co-operation with other denominations of Christians. It ii a pleasing feature of the present ser- vice that representatives of so many Other bodies are with us. We can all help each other. There is ample room for all our energies, and earnest need for hearty co-operation. We shall each find fitting occasion to ! advance our own peculiar views. And there is truth, more or Was, on the side of all of us. But while we hold and advocate our distinctive tenets we can live end love as brethren. If ever! can render service to other churches than my own, it will be a pleasui e to me so to do; and I trust that frequent occasions will arise when fraternity such as lessen to-night nosy again andegein be displayed. As regards the town itself, in which my lot is not wilwci be a , I- pleasure o p e ttoomeprtoovtea k ae usetul ',habitant. My general views of truth are tielined, practically, by the fact that I am a Con- gregational ininiater, and also by the futther fact that this Church has deeme lit wise t entrust it to my care. I take it for granted that my general adhesion to truths ordinarily believed by ee•angelical Christi ma is un- derstood. I bust that it will be found that on all matters essential I have an intelligent faith, and that W y teaching will embody these truths. I desire to Preach Christ, the living loving Saviour, the revealer of the Father, the redeemer of the world. I shall aim to lead men to Him, to gather young and old beneath His cross, and then to en- list them as followers in His train. I hope to utter no uncertain sound, to preach nothing I do not believe, while, at the tame time, I desire myself to be ever learning, and se gamey's coming to a larger and inMiledsl PIG MAUI I GIG POI 14; . .

1 widest and truest theology is by any means perfect. I here is yet, as said the old Pilgrim Fathers "more light and truth to break forth from God's work." The future may disclose the error of much we now regird as true, and the truth of some we now deem error. But we need have no fear. God is "Ha own inter- preter," and He will make His own truth plain to human understanding in the right time and way. My diligent effort will be to teach men truth that shall save and bless them. Hearing first and most of the great teacher Himself, I shall strive to help others to this better knowledge; and my work will reward m I as I see that men and women and children gather strength and comfort and gladness and knowledge from my ministry, and as I see that the Church of Jesus Christ in this place is built up, increased, and strengthened. PLIANOIIISSTER, SATURDAY.—The progress of the week's business leads to believe that the chemical trade will become quieter the nearer approach to the ead of the year. This, of course, must be in a measure anticipated, and need cause no uneasiness, especially after the unwonted briskness of the past two months. The disposition ti weakness of a few articles which we noted in our last has deepened, and it is possible to obtain these at slightly lower quotations. Taking the market in its entirety, however, and remembering the period of the year, there is a firmness ruling in prices which is eminently satisfactory. Inquiries for forward contracts are less numerous, kwhile those for prompt, though fairly sustained, cannot he entertained for execution at a moment's notice. Thus a more inquiring spirit in respect of future business would be appreciated on the one hand, while on the other manufacturers are not in a position to entertain orders to any great extent for execution within the limited present.

CoAL.—General complaints of depression in the coal trade of this district continue to be made. Although the better sort of round coal still meet with a tolerably good demand, there is nothing like the usual pressure for supplies at this season of the year, and the ordin- ary output at the pits is, as a rule, quite sufficient to meet the present requirements without any necessity to fall back upon stocks. Second qualities of coal meet with a moderate inquiry, and best burgy is not d.fficult to sell; but inferior descriptions of round coal for steam purposes and common classes ef engine fuel are a drug in the market, and considerable stocks are accumulating on the pit banks, the supplies of slack especially being considerably in excess of the demand. The average pit prices in tne Wigan district range about as under Lest Arley, Ils. to 121. per ton ; Porn. berton four-feet, 9s. to 9s. 81. per ton; common round 004, 7a. to 83.; burgy, ô. 3d. te 6s. 6d.; ordinary slack, 3s. to 43. per ton.

IBON.—The near approach of the Christmas holidays is causing rather a lull in the iron trade of this district. Lancashire makers hold eisnsidernble stocks of pig iron. They are very stiff in their quotations, which re. main at 675. per ton for No. 3 foundry and 663. to 66e. per ton for No. 4 forge, delivered into the Manchester district. Other brands of iron offering here are with- out material change; Lincolnshire iron being quoted at 675. 66. to 68s. 66. per ton for No. 3 foundry, and 66e. 6d. to 665, 61. per ton for No. 4 forge, and Middles. borough iron at 643. 9d. to 65. 9d. per ton for N 0.3 zoundry, 645. 3d. to 641. 9.1. for No. 4 foundry, and 535. 91. for No. 4 forge, delivered into this district. Finished iron continues firm in price, the majority of the forge proprietors being still pretty well occupied, and for good local bars delivered into the Manchester district £7 17s. 6d. to £7 per ton is asked.

GREAT REFORM UNION MEETING.
SPEECH OF MR. G. W. LATHAM.

The annual meeting of the General Council of the National Reform , Unionovas held in Manchester Town Hell, on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. d. Slagg, chairman of the executive committee, presiding. The committee, in their report, reviewed the work of the year, and expressed gratification at the steady and continuous growth of the organisation, and its oonstant and large accession of power. At present 750 affiliated and corresponding clubs are included in the Union, and almost every day brings an accession of power The committee also recorded their regret at the deaths of Sir Elkanali Armitage, Mr. Thomas Thomasson, and Mr. Elijah Dixon. In the evening, a large public) meeting was held in the Free-trade Hall, Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., in the chair. Resolutions were passed Calling upon the Government to act in conformity with the expressed wishes of the people in reference to the Eastern Question, protesting against the continued exclusion of large numbers of householders in the United 'Kingdom from the exercise of the franchise, and supporting the objects of the National Reform Union. Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., Mr. Hopwood, M.P., Mr. B. Whitworth. M.P., Mr. 11. Lee, Mr. G. W. Latham, Mr. Samuelson, and Mr. j. Arch were among the speakers. Mr. G. W. Lamm, of Bradwall Hall, Sandbaoh, who was received with great cheering, sponded the following resolution, which had been Any moved by- the Rev. D. S. Prosser, of Crewe—" That this meeting calls upon her Majesty's Government to act in con- formity with the expressed wiehes of the people of England, by abstaining from any further support of the Turkish Government, and direct its policy towards the establishment of free government and representa- tive institutions for the subject populations of the Christian provinces of the Porte." Mr. Latham said After the most eloquent speech that I have just heard, and after the introductory remarks of the Chairman, I should be vain indeed if I imagined that any words of mine were likely to cause greater unanimity in this meeting than, I am quite certain, will be gained by what has already been said. (Applause.) As I believe Manchester has already held, from the beginning of the discussion of the Eastern question to the present time, at least four public meetings, and as the conclusions at those meetings are those to which the resolution points, I think it would be merely wasting your time and wearying out my voice if I ventured to make any remarks on a suljeat which seems already settled. (Cheers, and cries of" Go on.") Not a man, or hardly a single town or village in England—l will not ex- cept that historic village of Hugbenden, at which our present Premier lives, where if a testing were held not carefully packed by Conservative tickets .--which would not come to the same con- clusion as I expect you will do to-night. (Cheers.) Ladies and gentlemen, it does seeem to me, however, that the vniter of the resolution put into my heads to second has been somewhat of a bumourist, and in- tended the Ministry to commit a great practical joke. Of all men the Fuck is about the cleverest and best diplomatist, and pretty well aware of what is going on in England, Therefore, what a prime joke it would be if some Perdu' on receiving the resolution which the Minister was requested to send him—asking for the establishment in Turkey of representative in- stitutions and free Gevernment—replied "Physician heal thyself." That might be a very proper answer to the Turko-Disraeli Government. (Laughter.) First, perhaps, we should say, you must make no distinction In religion, the Christian must be equal to the Maher- sultan. Dc n't you think the Pasha might whisper back and ask—" Are there no distinctions of religion in Eng. land, and are not you, as a Government, fostering and keeping up those distinodons in every possible way t (Cheers.) Have you not in England a privileged Church which takes the whole revenue of the State. while the others are left out in the cold I"' It is true my Lord Salisbury that in your churchyards the dead of different creeds are treated on a totally different footing, and the minister of one religion not allowed to enter there and'ssy the last words of farewell over the bodies of their own Sankt Surely the demand for the equal treatment of all religious creeds would come but badly from a Ministry which had been backing up such Iniquities in England. (Cheers.) Taoll we are going to ask the Tusks to give their subjects free govern. meat. Have we free government in England at the present moment F living, as I do, In the country, I doubt it vary much—at least solar as the rural parts are concerned. I see that the governors of the district In which I live are not appoiuted by the people in any way, but are simply the creatures of the Lord Lientene ant, nominated at his own will, because of their poli- ties and nothing more. (Hear, hear.) I have seep., and seen to my c at, men rejected, because their opinions were not coincident with those of the ruling powers. Where have you got representative institutions in England F True, we have got them in towns, but we have not yet got them in the country. Mr. Arch— (cheers)—whose voice you will hear to-night, will tell you, much better than I can hope to do, what the facts of the ease are, how many millions in England are unrepresented at the present time; and he can tell you how, so far as the finances of every c3unty go, they are not administered by the ratepayers, but by a totally outside body. (Shame.) This Government is totally incapable for these reasons, if for no other, of urging on Turkey thorough reform so far se regards their proceedings in the provinces. (Cheers.) This brings me to this point, a point I would have you think or n ost seriously—in 1874, that disastrous elec- tion for the Liberal party. After the election in 1874 there were hundreds and hundreds of us ready to say that it does not matter if a Tory Government is in office a short time. They will do no harm, and the Liberal party will have time to think what our future movements shall be, and to close up our ranks. Others said it does not matter, we could not carry our pet crotchets, and we shall probably carry them under, a Tdry Government:. Some said it served the Liberals right for not having allowed particular sections of their followers to carry out their pet crotchets, and it was right to leave them out in the cold a bit. The crotcheteers now understand the mistake they made. I say, it is always bad for the country when a Tory Government is in office. The time must come when a Liberal Government will be wanted; when men will be wanted who are capable of grasping great emergencies, and who will not go on peddling and tinkering, and trying to botch up affairs, with the hope that there may be peace in their own—or as Mr. Freeman purit. during their tenure of office. (Cheers.) We must have at all times a government whom we can trust, and not one which, confessedly, as Lord Derby said the other day, wants to know the opinion of its employers before it acts. (Hear, hear.) A govern- ment consisting of twelve charity boys would be cap- able of governing this country if they were told what to do. (Laughter and cheer'.) We don't want a government for us to govern, bat a government to govern us. (Cheers.) Ido trust that at any future election we shall give up, so far as is necessary, each and all of us our individual crotchets or whims, and merge them in the one thought of how best to betleil the country. (Cheers.) The Reform Union has sett forth a programme. We do not believe that at the present moment every Liberal accepts that programme, but we know that it is really and truly a Liberal pro- gramme, and that ultimately all Liberals will accept it. As far as we can ascertain, the msj ority of Liberals are now in its favour. But if an election comes, let ell in favour of progress merge ,their individual ideas into the one great thought of how best to unite the Liberal party. The men at Manchester gloriously solved that problem at the beginning of the year, when they replaced Mr. Bright in the position he ought never to have lost, of member for this city. (Cheers.) Let all Liberals endeavour to do the same, and let the representatives of the Reform Union in other towns, as was done in your own tow., sink their differences. Then throughout the whole of England We May hope to get such a majority in the House of Corn- pious as will enable us to get rid of these governors who want to be governed, and put in their places men whom the entire country can trust; whose i vvo.ces would he heard in the courts of Europe; erh,s e would have some influence in persuading the Turokic:s do what is right, and in encouraging those countrie°s who with to join us, but have been kept off by the sneers and threate of the present Ministry, to help us 113 allies instead of working against us as enemies, (Ureat and prolonged cheering.) The resolution was carried with great enthusiasm.

SALE AMATEUR DRAMATIO ATM.

The vitality and prevalence of private theatricals seems to prove—if anything uttered by the great father of the English theatre required any proof—that " all the world's a stage, and all the men and women are Merely pl.q.irs." Whether the instinct for the stage is a kind of mutiny against this tyranny of cir- cumstance and is born of an ignorant envy of a condi. tioil which is other than our own, and seems brighter or happier than ours, it were possibly idle to inquire too curiously. Certain it is that Princes and Princesses have often been found " mummiug " as shoperds and aheperdesses, whilst less brilliantly placed persons have loved to glitter for an hour as emperors and great com- manders, although the actors did not "the division of a battle know more than a spinster." Can it be that there really is something in the doctrine of the trans+ migration of souls, and that most of us possess in dim rudimentary form the 'characters which we most affect to personate.. But this can hardly be, for a ver- satile actor would in that way, be

"A man so various that he seems to be Not one, but all the world's epitome." Something too much of this. It is certainly not need- ful that in writing a line or two about the performances of the Sale Amateur Dramatic Club on Friday and Saturday last, that we should play the philosopher; and play it "Indifferent well. The performance took place in the Drill Room, at Sale, and consisted of the comedy by Tom Taylor, "The )3abes in the Wood," and the coolie drama "The Spitalfields Weaver." The plot of " The Babes "is clever enough, but too complex and involved for narrative, but it has KlEL- client point and sparkle to interest and amuse. Ama- teurs like it, and those who like amateurs usually like it; and it is fair to say that the characters, in the hands of Messrs. Lynill, Itumsey, Pagden, Fowler, Lloyd, and others—not to speak of the ladies, whose precedence in this instance it is to be preceded, issued from the ordeal successfully. The comedietta of the " Interval " was capitally played, and consisted of a single scene of the most cordial congratulation. The " Spitalfields Weaver " followed the breadly humour. ous farce which has been made generally familiar by Mr. Toole. The farce, however, was played probably before Mr. Toole was born, and was specially written for the benefit of the Spitalfiolds weavers, who at that time were in dire distress. The performance was under the patronage of the Queen, who, if we remem- ber rightly, was present on the first night. The char- acter of " Brown " the weaver, made suddenly rich, an.l struggling with the usages of fashionable society, was tolerably well played by Mr. Daniels, who, how- ever, was much too genteel for the part, and ignored the weaver too persistently. " Simmons," who visits " Brown," and is a weaver all over, was made very droll by Air. Rumsey. Indeed, the acting all round merited praise ; but as these amateurs are not likely to apply to the stage manager of the Haymarket for lucrative engagements there, we shall refrain from writing to Mr. Coe on that subject. As for- the ladies, they are all born actresses and cannot help it, thank goodness.

This case was before the Chancery Division on Wed- nesday, It was a case in which the plaintiffs are tenants of chemical works upon a piece of land known se Widnes Marsh, on the Mersey, and the bll is filed against the defendant, who is the common landlord, to restrain him from closing up or in any way interfer- ing with their drainage, which now takes place by means of an open channel called the Marsh Brook. The plaintiffs' case is that by the reclamation works which are now going on the landlord is narrowing the chan- nel, and thereby obstructing that free flow of water in the brook which is necessary to carry off the chemical compounds discharged into the brook, and to prevent a deposit which would in time close up the channel altogether. On the other side, it is argued that the plaintiffs have no right to drain into the Marsh Brook at all, and if they have, that the deposits are of their own making, and are not the fault of the landlord. A number of witnesses have been called on the part of the plaintiff, who said that unless there was a proper flow of water the deposits were of such a character as would eventually fill up the brook, and they alleged that the defendant was not keeping such an open chan- nel as he ought to do. The witnesses were crosa.ex. mined at great length with the view of showing that some of the obstructions had been made with the object of making a passage for the workmen across the brook, or for the purpose of damming back the water whilst necessary works were being carried out. 1 The watcher of the drains and flushing, however, said he did not know this to he the ease, although he knew that improvements had been made along the brook. In re-examination he said the ridges were very hard, and, although portions were carried away by flushing, they formed again directly. The new system of flush- ing was not completed until this year, and without a slose watch and continual flushing the brook must eventually close up. Mr. Thomas Vickers, of the firm .of Vickers and Bons, superphosphate of lime manu- facturers, at Manchester, and having works at Widnes also gave evidence. He mid they held their works under the Hutchinson trustees, and drained into the brook in question, but threw nothing into it which would be likely to choke it.—Mr. Amos Anson, surve- yor, of St. Helens said the natural fall of the brook taken from a point 1440 yards from the Mersey was 4 feet 9 inches, and explained the effects of the tide upon the stream.—The plaintiffs' ease was not concluded at the rising of the court, and the further hearinf was adjourned until next Tuesday.—Mr. Kay, Q. 0., Sir H. Jackson, Q.C., and Mr. Beale appeared for the plain- tiffs ; and hlr. Fry, Q. 0., Mn, Milward, Q. 0., Mn, Macroy, and Mr. Methued for the defendant.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, a boy named Smith, fourteen years of age, together with six or seven others, was charged with breaking into two shops on 'Sunday, and with stealing a quantity of goods. It appears that Smith, who has been frequently in prison, is the leader of a gang of young thieves, and Is known by the name of" The Captain." At the Liverpool Assizes on Friday, Elizabeth Large, aged 28, a married woman, was indicted for the man- slaughter of her child, George Large, aged ten months. Mr. Shand prosecuted; the prisoner was undefended. It was stated that the prisoner was a woman given to drinking to excess, and that on the 19th August last she and her mother were in a public house in Widnes, and drank a good deal together. The child was with them, and after they had been in the house a con- siderable time the prisoner left, taking the child with her. Next morning, the 20th, she returned home to her house in Church-street, Widnes, without the child. Her mother made inquiries, and found that the prisoner had slept all night in a privy, and that, whilst drunk, she had let the child fall into the privy. Its body was afterwards found there, and the prisoner was apprehended. The mother of the prisoner, in her evidence, said that on the night in question the husband of the prisoner beat her and two of her children, and that he threatened to beat witness, and she had to sleep in an empty house that night with another of the prisoner's children.—The jury found the prisoner guilty.—His Lordship said it was impossible to regard the occurrence as an accident. The funeral of Mr. Jonathan Wilson, whose death we noticed In our laet Josue, took place at Runcorn Parish Church, on Monday morning last, when a large number of townspeople and friends assembled to pay tribute of respect to ,tho deceased gentleman's memory. During the morning the shops in the town I were closed, and amongst tradespeople busineee seemed generally suspended. At the funeral were the leading inhabitants of the town, the chairman and members of the Runcorn Commissioners, the Freemasons of which order the deceased gentleman was a member, and the licensed victuallers. The funeral service was impressively read by the vicar, the Rev, Canon Barclay. •

Land's Fo.d hasT.ieen reached, we must sow return home. A quiet Sunday after our hard though pleasant week was a true Sabbath. We strolled to Madron the parent church of Penzance, we visited the Wesley-rock chapel, built over the rock from which the great preacher addressed the Cornish miners by thousands and turned Cornwdll into a "land of saints." In Madron churchyard is a laconic biography on a tomb. stone—that of George. Daniell the founder of the Schools:—

" Belgia me birth, Britaine me breeding gave, Cornwall a wife, ten children and a grave." What more does anyone but a genius want P There are few John sons who needßoswella, and churchyards are not the places where ones praises should be trune- ted. Soon, however, like the Parisian assembly where a man was distinguished by not wearing a decoration, a tombstone will be peculiar by not.,having on it a ful- some panegyric.

One of our party heard a sermon on iL fidelity, in which there was a neat remark on the attempts to ex- plain the mysteries of nature on merely materialistic principles. The preacher said, scientific explanations were only the consonants of the zeal meaning. The words were inaudible, meaning lees without the sid.of the vowels supplied by religion. Ido ipjusl ice to the preacher, in putting it so clumsily, but that is the 'gist of his remark.

Our object being to return by the North Coast of Cornwall and Devon, we went by train as far as Grampound-road, passing Hayle, with St. Ives' Bay in the distance, Camborne In the centre of.a wonderfully rich mining district, Redruth, a dirty busy looking town, also depending on the mining industry foriit a prosperity, and Truro. At Grarnpound-road, we took a wagonette, and struck off for the coast which we reached at blawgan Forth. Here is a wide expanse of sand bordered by rocks that are tunnelled into caves. A walk along the coast brought us to Bedruthian Of all she lovely spots we saw in Cornwall, Bed- ruthian is the lovelisst. " Ferat, qui meruit palmam ;" and it certainly does bear the palm. The variety of the coast scenery, the grandeur and confusion of the scattered rooks, the extent and beauty of the sands, the curious outlying islands, so irregular in size, shape, and position, they look as if .they have bassi dropped in sport by some gigantic hands—ell combine with a quietness and simple beauty which is fascinating to d degree. Some of the rocks assume curious shape ; one lofty peak is exactly like the pictures of Queen Elizabeth. Were you to see the prints of it, you would soy they were not true to stature, Bo complete likeness are they of what we are accustomed to see as portraits of Uood Queen Bess. But the photographs are the same, with crown, nil!, and farthingale, all complete.

We were ascending the steepethough wide ascent which gives its name to the Steps of Bestruthian, when we were accosted by a voice that seemed familiar to us. It was that of one who had crossed our path more than once. He was t •avelling as the representative of a Sanitary Company, called, I think, the Goux system. He was a kind hearted, sensible man, but rather too full of his subject. Though I .have a great interest in sanitary matters, when the inerite of a drainage eye. tern is continually forced down your throat, in your walks and at your dinner, it is anything but plea- slut. 'Toulouse perdrix," as the Fcench say, and when the "partridge" is sauitition "Goux" this, and "Glaux"• that, it becumee more than unsavoury. In proposing a toast, the joker of our party ventured to hope that the time would come when it would be "Chemin son gout" (Lima). After this doubtful com- pliment, we separated. What glorious baths we had on those Cornish coasts! No men, women, and children prowling about, no horrie toothless machines, none of the forbidding para- phernalia of places like ithyl or Southport, a cave for our dressing-room, and only the sea birds in the blue eky to look on. How exhitarateng! One of our party with more than r priukling of grey hairs in his head, in a fit of entrusiaein, putting himself into a classical attitude, burst forth "Toe &Wish youth, disporting itself on Britain's shores I " We rested that right at St. Colonab• Here is the largest church in Cornwall, and there was some talk of making it the seat of the new bishopric, a privilege now given to Intro. We lodged in the house of one Polkinghorne, the sou of the famous Cornish wrestling champion. Very obliging, vary eutertaiuing, and very intelligent was this son of Milan. He was grieved that wrestling should be losing favour, and offered to take us the next day where we might still see it practised, at some village sports. He was a strong-looking man, and spoke with such practical energy.ot the " Polkinge borne grip" as to make some of us rather nervous, lest his excitement should lead him to show us, experimen- tally, its force. Oaly one place more of importance and we have visited as much of Cornwall as we iuteuded. We are bound to ate sohg-farnous Tintagel, the home of Arthur and his knights, 'Many towered Camelot." • Leaving St. Colomb, we went by comeh to Camelford, a smell town disfranchised by the Reform Bill of 1632, passing eothing very interesting on our way, except Wade Bridge the longest and most venerable in Corn- wall. From Cameltord we walked to Tintagel. quiet, lovely, spot is Tintagel. The neat little inn was occupied by a large family of visitors, very agreeable; and a couple on their honeymoon, who with the selfishness of supreme happiness, thought only of themselves. A walk of ten minutes -brought us to the castle. It must have been a wonderfully strong place, this glorious castle of Tintagel, but now i there s little of it left. Still, you can see from its situation on the very brink of a precipice 300 feet above the sea, forming the extremity of a bold pro. montory, almost separated from the main land by the dashing of the waters, that it justifies Leland's des scription ;—" A marvelous strong and notable fort- ereeee, and almost situ loci inexpugnabile." Hence ' issued forth Prince Arthur and his knights. He who is at all- influenced by poetry and noble deeds cannot but feel touched by the sight. I plead guilty to being somewhat matter-of-fact ; „ but as I thought of the legends of the British heroes, how they run through the whole of our English literature, how

- • how Gower, Chaucer, Shakespeare, Bulwer Lytton, and our sweet.tongued Tennyson have drawn inst ira- tion from them—when I thought that this was the place, whence sallied forth Arthur, the peerless knight and king, accompanied by modest Gawain, noble Lannoe. lot and gentle Tristram, I saw the reflected light of ' heroio deeds, and almost thought 1 stood on holy ground. There are now few traces of the buildings. The glory is departed, and even the beauty -of the situ. ation is marred by the presence of milling apparatus close to the foot of the lofty rock. Verily, the things of commerce are prosaic. On the whole, we decided that the northern coast of Cornwall is to be preferred by the tourist to the south, In spite of tho oharms of the Lizard, The climate is less enervating, the scenery is bolder, the place is less infested with tourists, and Bedruthian is unapproach. able. We made our way home, along the north coast of Devon, taking the coach to Bade, thence to Clo- velly, the " hanging village," and on to Bideford and Westward no. At Bideford we oAt train to Exeter, and thence to London and Warri, gton. Havel fulfilled my promise of pointing out to your readers au excursion worthy of a Wel ? If these letters assist any Warringtonians to enjoy a pleasant tour, I shall be rewarded.

div.p: UNITARIANIM AT RUNCORN.

The Rev. H. W. PerriE, of Warrington, delivered the third of the advertise.: series of lectures at the Pub. ho Hall, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening. 'I he room was crowded, and the audience very attentive. At th commencement of the proceedings Mr. Perris read an anonymous note he had received, in which a tract was enclosed; the title "What must I do to be saved.', He credited }is correspondent with the kinder motives, but pointed out that the act implied a coo assurance of the writeee own infallibility, and a singn- lar forgetfialness of the facts which lay on the surface of the present movement. The lecture, which bad been &livered on "Salvation might be erroneous but it embodied a very wide experience, and a thorough knowledge of orthodox evangelicallem in all ita various and discrepant forms; experience gained .borli in Episoopaltan and Nonconformist cirri( s. When earnest enquiry and cosily struggle had led him without the camp, was it likely that anonymous appeals and tracts with which be had all his life been familiar, would revels° the verdict of hie reason and conscience and lead him back again p The lecture was a frank and familiar exposition of the theme " Renouncing Orthodoxy to follow Christ." Mr. Perris examined the dogma of "the Fall" at considerable length, shew. - kg that it was at variance with the simplest and most assured facts of science and history, which taught the rise of man from very feeble beginnings, and explained the progress of civilisation as the gradual development of a Divine put pose, and the education of humanity for the kingdom of heaven—the Paradise not of the past, but of the future. It is to be regretted that as the lecturer made his way to the cab which was in wait. lag, to enable him to catch his train, some rowdy per- sons struck up "Hold the fort," and taunted him with cowardice in not remaining till midnight, even rune - wog after the cab, and howling as it drove away. This, too, although Mr. Perris hid told them at the outset that he had not reached home till one o'clock that morning. in consequence of his good-natured willingness to hold discussion at Earlestown. The respectable persons of Runcorn will doubtlees purge themselves of any complicity with such behaviour.

It is stated that discussion will be invited after the Lecture by the Rev. Richard Pitcher, 8.A., to be delivered on Wednesday next, and hope has been az. pressed that Orthodox intereete will fall into worthy and competent handl.

div.p: TEE MADMA.N'S OTJTRAGE AT FRODBHAM.

At the Chester Assizes, on Friday, before Mr, Justice Mellor, Thomas Holmes, 27, striker, Gersten, was in. dicted for feloniously assaulting, wounding, and ill. treating Aaron Jeremiah Ellis, with intent to kill and murder him on the 24th Nov., and further with it- tempzieg to commit suicide by throwing himself under a railway carriage on the Cheshire junction railway, at Frodsham, oa the same data. Mr. Swetenlainn prosecuted, and Mr. Marshall appeared for the pie sonar, who had his arm in a sling, he having not yet recovered from the injuries he received in the conflict. The prosecutor was travelling from Liverpool to Chester, and when the train was near Frodsham the prisoner jumped up, and suddenly attacked Mr. Ellis In a ferocious manner, end bit his thumb off, and was about to cut his throat, when the prosecutor and the prisoner's father overpowered him The prisoner then jumped out of the carriage and tried to ()manna suicide by throwing himself under the wheels, but the train having been stopped, the guard prevented him from carrying out his intention. The prosecution alleged that the prisoner was suffering from delirium tremens, arising from excersive drinking. The defence was that the prisoner's insanity was produced by excessive grief, be having Lost his wife under palatal circumstances, only a few days before the outrage, and the excessive grief produced acute mania. After other evidence had been adduced, Mr. Bwetene ham said that the evidence for the defence had con- vinced him that there was no proof the prisoner had been drinking. The Judge said the learned counsel had taken a very creditable course. Tne evidence for the defence must have struck them all with great force. The whole demeanour of the man showed that ho was ailing either from delirium tremens, in which case there would have been no defence, or else from an attack of acute mania. Every man was liable for any act when suffering under a paroxysm brought on by a voluntary act, but in this case the evidence showed that the prisoner was in a state of mania brought on by an excess of acute private grief. The jiver then, uuder the direotiun of hie Lordship, returned a verdict of aeguittal on the ground of in. sanity, He was ordered to be detained in custody until proper evidence of his sanity was given to the autho• cities.

div.head: NEW FORTS FOR THE MERSEY
div.p: NEW FORTS FOR THE MERSEY
AND ERWELL.

Sciamss for deepening the Irwell so as virtually to make it a tidal river which would admit of sea-going vessels reaching Manchester, have been mooted from time to time for many years past. Latterly the same subject has occasionally been broached in a vague and inconsequential way. Para- 1 graphs have appeared in the press, accom- panied by comments of a not unfavourable and quasi-official character, but we have not met with any formulated prospectus or technical projection of any such undertaking. That may be owing to our own lack of knowledge, and it is quite possible that should such a scheme be in the course of in- cubation with any chance of success in the way of hatching, prospectuses, plans, and estimates, which may be at present pigeon- holed, and lying perdu, would very soon see the light. That such a project is feasible enough from an engineering point of view, we have no doubt. It would be rash to put a limit upon any physical work which cannot be accomplished by modern engineering science. Not to mention the stupendous deeds in that way in the shape of supplying towns with water, in preventing cities being entirely submerged by water, in bridging not merely rivers but arms of the sea, and tunnelling mountain ranges, and ocean straits, we can see what has been done much nearer home by such works as making a railway across a quaking bog like Chat Moss, and that intrepid work of Brindley's, the Bridgewater Canal. As a case more im- mediately in question we may also mention the deepening of the Clyde, so as to allow ocean-going vessels to ascend as far as the Bromielaw, in the contra of the City of Glas- gow. Without in the least detracting from the success of these great projects, and practicable and simple enough as the scheme for deepening the Irwell, to the extent pro- posed, seems, we must confess that we do not see our way to its feasibility from a com- mercial point of view. In that sense the difficulties appear to us to be insurmount- able.

We presume that no one would think of proposing such a scheme unless it was in- tended to pay, as a commercial speculation. We should not dare to say here what expen- diture would be required to bring it to a successful issue from first to last, but no doubt the outlay would be something enor- mous, and so far as we can see, far surpas- sine any advantages pecuniary or otherwise which could be expected to be derived from it. It the first place, enormous interests would have to be bought off, and here we may say that whatever might have been its chances of success at one time of converting Manchester into a seaport like Glasgow, it is now too late in the day to think of it. No one in his senses !would even dream of sea- going vessels going up the Irwell to the centre ofManchester, demolishing the bridges and doing away with the traffle between Manchester and Salford. In the first place then, the ships would have to remain farther down the stream, say at Mode-Wheel or Throstle Nest, thus losing a great deal of the assumed advantages to ibegin with. Again, we suppose that Liverpool would have some- thing to say in the shape of tolls and town- dues. These are two formidable obstacles to begin with, but what is to be gained, putting them aside altogether? Is it a saving of expense, by doing away with Liverpool charges in. the ;shape of dock expenses, middlemen, commissions and so forth? Or is it by saving similar charges in Manchester by sending goods on board ship there, instead of delivering them over to the carriers who convey them to Liverpool either by railway or canal ? Superficially and upon paper it looks plausible enough that these charges might be saved or at least reduced, but we are not so sure that that would in reality be the fact, supposing the project to a fait accompli. We must bear in mind that Man- chester is not Lancashire, and that so far as cotton is concerned, it is not increasing but taken in conjunction with the increase of its population, it has positively decreased as a manufacturing town. True, it is the depet of the surrounding towns for the sale of their cotton fabrics, and so far as that is concerned cotton goods and yarns sold to go abroad might be packed in Manchester and shipped there. But all the goods and yarns sold to go abroad are not sent to Liverpool, but vast quantities to Grimsby and .Hull. Then again, in the way of receiving raw cotton in bales, supposing that spinners imported all their own cotton, which they don't, nor a tenth or fiftieth part of it. Is it to be supposed that cotton to be consumed by Preston, Bolton, Wigan, Stockport, Oldham, Blackburn, Burnley, Rochdale, Ashton, Stalybridge, and other towns, would be sent to Manchester ,in preference to Liverpool? Not exactly. It is just as convenient for the manufacturers of these towns to get their cotton from Liverpool as it would be from Manchester. Moreover, it suits their pur- pose better to go to Liverpool, because it is the great central market of the world for cotton, where its price is regulated, and where the proious staple ct.n be turned into cash at one price or another at a few minutes notice. To such a degree is this the case, that a spinner who has im- ported a lot of cotton, almost always has it sampled and over-hauled in Liverpool by his own broker before it is forwarded to so that he may know how he stands an !whether the quality is suitable for him. So much fo'r receiving cotton by ship in Manchester. If it t'!!‘l not suit the spinner as to quality, what is he to nl; with it? Send it back to Liverpool in order to be hU Where then is the saving as regards ex- I pense? --

Manchester could never supersede Liver- pool as a shipping port, It could only interfere with it in the most infinitesimal degree, and with little or no advantage to itself. It has the advantage of bonding warehouses already. Where then are the profits to come from for the expenditure of making the river navigable for sea-going vessels? We have only referred to cotton and cotton goods, but the same remarks apply in a great measure to groceries and hard goods imported from abroad. The fact is that goods are despatched from the Manchester warehouses for shipment at present, with very little trouble, and upon a well regulated system which works smoothly and economically. The goods are packed, the carrier calls for them and sees to their being forwarded either by rail or by canal, the latter preferred unless great haste ia re- quired as being more secure, and less exposed to damage. Lighters take them alongside the outgoing vessel, on wnich they are put forthwith, and there is an end of them for the time. Manchester may be made a sea- port at some future time, but it will not be in our day. The bold if not audacious saying that "Science is the Providence of Man," might be wholly true, judging by the supreme importance which of late is attached to scientific discovery. The " endowment of research" is a subject indeed that has lately ob- tained much public consideration, and a combination for this object of the state endowment principle with the voluntary system is already in conspicuous operation, for it appears that the Royal Society has now considerable funds at its disposal for the pur- pose of promoting scientific research. It has the Handley bequest of £6,000, Mr. Carrington's £2,000 Mr. Dircks's £B7B, Sir C. Wheatstone's £5OO, (added to the Wollaston), and the splendid gift by Mr Jodrell of £6,000 specially for original research. The Government have promised £4,000, besides the usual grant of £l,OOO for five years, and it appears that recommendations are to be made to the Lord President of the Council, which will include personal allowances or grants of money. After all, money so invested may return a hundred fold. Science has achieved so much during the last century in the economy of labour, that it is possible to understand that the price of a single ironclad wisely expended might ultimately prove to be an economy of millions. Substitutes for gas are being frequently discussed— especially in Warrington—where the Corporation went to buy the gas works, and the opponents of, the purchase talk of the scientific possibility of gas becoming an obsolete illuminator—and if the light of future days were suddenly to issue from the laboratery of endowed research, science would have wrought its latest miracle, and nobody would grumble at the cost of it.

Looking at the famine of harmless pleasure under which the working folk of this, the most industrious country in the world, groans and go to the deuce, and at the same time endeavour foolishly and vainly to alleviate by an antidote which has become a national bane—the public-house—one reads with a puzzled eagerness the remarks of Bishop Fraser, who, In a sermon delivered last Sunday, said something about music and dancing for the people. Adverting to the places in our large towns where the people thronged for this kind of amusement, the Bishop pointed out its danger to young persons, as it was at present surrounded.. Speaking generally of this sort of popular amusement, "he said he was not one of those ascetics who said that dancing was a damning sin. He had danced himself when he was young, and if he were to say that it was a damning sin he should be telling all the fashionable people who went to the Assembly Rooms at Cheetham Hill Road that they were going "to the Pit," and that the well-to-do persons who went to Halle's concerts did so at the peril of their souls. He did not talk such nonsense as that, for he did not believe in it. everyone He thought there were places where recreation of that kind could be enjoyed under conditions of safety, and he further urged that it was the duty of purify such places order to make them safe veryfeveryonee the young." in When one remembers that recreation is as much a necessary of healthy life as bread is, and that the hunger for it is almost as difficult to appease, one cannot regret that a gentle- man in lawn sleeves, and who, at any rate, seems to have the courage of his opinions, does not share that episcopal timidity which seems to afflict every British bishop with what Mr. Bright would call a "creeping paralysis" on all subjects directly affecting the welfare and happiness of the people of England. Mr. Gladstone must now regret that he did'rit make a few more bishops of the complexion of "J. Man- chaster."

It is not every Conservative member of Parliament who can be so candid about the Prime Minister as Mr. Dalrymple, M.P. for Bute, who, speaking a few days since at Rothesay, said "he thought it unfor- tunate that at a critical period, when the words of statesmen were carefully weighed, Lord Beaconsfield should manage in every speech to say something which perplexed the country, and which required all the wisdom and ability of his eminent colleagues who commanded confidence to rectify." Mr. Dal- rymple's political accuracy is scarcely equal to his courage. The "eminent colleagues" of the Prime Minister do not "rectify " the speeches of Lord Beaconsfield. It is the country which rectifies that heedless and perilous rhetoric.

The Altrincham magistrates must have been con. siderably puzzled on Monday last by the "Dog Inn" case of Messrs. Greenall, the brewers, of Warrington. The "Dog Inn," which is at Heat. ley, was adjudged to have lost its license, at a meeting of magistrates held on the 9th of October last, by reason of one Egan, the former tenant, de- dining to have the license if the Bench granted it. At that time Messrs. Greenall, it would appear-- although Egan was ejected. in July last—had no tenant for the house, and the Bench consequently refused to grant the license. Last Monday Mr. Taylor, a barrister, of Manchester, applied for the renewal of the license for Messrs. Greenall under another and a different Act of Par- liament, and succeeded in getting the license renewed. The old saying as to the possibility of driving a coach of sin through an Act of Parliament, seems to be curi- ously realised in this case, where it seems that one Act of Parliament can ride triumphantly over another. The Counsel in the "Dog Inn" case very aptly remarked that there is nothing on the English statute book so complicated as the Licensing Act, and that it was difficult if not impossible even for professional lawyers always to comprehend its intention. It is due, however, to the wonderful creatures, in London, to whom the framing of new Licensing Acts is so discreetly confided, to admit that they so cleverly plan their labyrinthine law that gentlemen of the Greenall persuasion invariably get the benefit of the doubt. By the way what was the meaning of the flippant reference by counsel to the new baronet of Wilders. pool brewery? This barrister—a Mr. Taylor, of Manchester—who appears to have been instructed in the "Dog Inn" case by Messrs. Davies and Brook, of Warrington, should have been duly im- pressed with the,political and other importance of,his patron's client. It was intolerable that this counsel should refer to Sir Gilbert Greenall, the head of the brewing firm—as "Sir Thomas—or something— "l " " something " indeed Think of Greena“ . s "Sir Something Greenam •

Sir,—Will yon permit me to enter my hearty protest against the conduct of a handful of rowdiel who dia. graced the town they live in and dishonoured the reli- gion they pretend to care for, by mobbing the Rev. Mr. Perris, of Warrington, on his way to the Railway Station, after delivering a lecture in Runcorn, last Wednesday evening. Although I happen to differ with the lecturer's opinions, as others may, I concede to him what I myself demand, feuedom of opinion Well-known and respected ministers of a cultivated and eminently philanthropic body like the Unitarians ought to have better treatment. They engage a Public Hall at their own expense, charge no admission fee, and make no collection. No one is obliged to go. Those who think it worth their while to do so ought to behave themselves. To be a Christian ought to be synonymous with being a gentleman. I hope that those who are able to influence the screaming tyrants of the gutter, of whom Runcorn has reason to complain, will point out to them that their conduct in the cue in question is little lees of an oetrage on public decency than that of the gentlemen of the" Cork Club," whose exploits lately received tome attention from the police authorities and the magistrates of Rancorn.—Yours, FAIR PLAY.
